title: The 60-Second Demo That Gets You AI Interviews
content:
Nobody hiring for AI roles is going to clone your repo and run it.
But they might watch a sixty-second video.
Here's how to make that video count.
Most people share a GitHub link and hope.
The recruiter opens it, sees a folder of files, and closes the tab.
Not because your work is bad, but because they can't see it working.
A short demo video fixes that.
First ten seconds. The problem.
One sentence about who has the pain.
"Support teams waste time searching documents for every ticket."
No tools yet. Just the problem.
Next twenty-five seconds. Show it working.
One real task, start to finish, on screen.
Type the question, show the answer, show the source.
Don't explain the code here. Let the product speak.
Now here's the part that makes you look senior instead of junior.
Next fifteen seconds. Show a failure.
Ask it something it can't answer, and show it saying "I don't know."
Or show the check that catches a bad answer.
Companies hiring for AI roles worry about wrong answers more than anything else.
Showing you planned for failure tells them you understand the real job.
Last ten seconds. The stack, one trade-off, and the link.
"I used a smaller model because it was fast enough and cheaper."
That one line shows judgment.
Where do you put it?
At the top of your README, pinned on your LinkedIn profile, and in every application message.
Record it on your laptop. Fancy editing is not needed.
Clear audio and a working product matter far more than music.
Then record a new one every time you ship a real improvement.
Your demo videos become a public timeline of your progress.
Here's my take. A working demo beats a long resume line.
Problem, working, failure, trade-off. Sixty seconds.
Follow for your daily AI update.
